Next: what a fixed-sphere contact law cannot capture

4Battery Materials Lab.
 Fixed-shape DEM limits and the material point method (MPM)
• Our fixed-shape implementation has no shape change and no yield cap: overlap is the only 
plasticity proxy; the softened SE modulus (1.35 vs ≈ 22 GPa) is an effective parameter, not a 
property [1, 2].
• J2 plasticity on a background grid: shape change and void filling that a fixed-shape sphere 
cannot represent; active material is kept rigid (DEM skeleton), only the electrolyte flows.

Next: from the compacted structure to a transport mesh

6Battery Materials Lab.
 Voxelizing the compacted microstructure into a transport mesh
• Faces are joined by a harmonic mean with no interface-resistance term: an ideal-interface 
voxel model — an upper bound only within the same geometry, properties and boundaries.
• VGCF as diameter-preserving segments, PTFE as a centre-line insulator, polymer as spheres; a 
registered 104-arm study keeps the σ(e⁻) order across 1–4 wt% VGCF on all tested grids 
(72/72).

7Battery Materials Lab.
 Composition-dependent porosity in five simulated beds
• Soft-sphere DEM with a linear hysteretic contact law, pressed to 300 MPa; one bed per 
composition, no seed replicates.
• One 7:3 bed: porosity 31.8 → 25.1 → 16.7 → 16.5 % (final state relaxed at fixed platen); 7:3 
(large : small NCM) is the lowest of the five beds.

Next: the same five beds as a Li⁺ contact network

8Battery Materials Lab.
 From the contact network to Li⁺ transport
• Contact-network approach [8]: bulk resistance + Holm/Maxwell constriction using Hertz 
contact radii; chosen σ₀ = 1.5 mS cm⁻¹ (pellet-literature range).
• Transport tortuosity T = φ_SE σ₀ / σ_eff: 7.2 → 5.0 (0:10 → 7:3). Contact constriction accounts 
for 73–75 % of Joule dissipation in this network model.

Next: what does not work — grid and absolute σ(e⁻)

9Battery Materials Lab.
 Problems 1 and 2: grid dependence and absolute σ(e⁻)
• The electronic ratio decreases across the three tested voxel spacings (0.4, 0.3, 0.25 µm); the 
ionic ratio crosses 1. Grid convergence has not been established.
• Voxel predictions exceed the available DC-polarization estimates; measurement conditions 
remain unverified. A registered re-run calibrates carbon on SBE alone (σ_VGCF* = 3.41 S cm⁻¹, 
an effective value); the DBE prediction (order only) is pending.
Limits

(c) NCM–SE beds: no carbon/binder; Hertz H0; common NCM reference 4.1 mS cm⁻¹ [11]; size factor off; one bed per composition.

Next: how load is shared between NCM and SE contacts

10Battery Materials Lab.
 Problem 3: Load sharing during compaction
• NCM–NCM contacts contribute 48–60 % of vertical stress after relaxation at fixed platen 
position; 7:3 is the minimum.
• The NCM–NCM stress-share ranking matches the experimental porosity summaries for the 
selected five compositions (exploratory, n = 5).

Next: what the nominal plate pressure contains

11Battery Materials Lab.
 Problem 4: what the 300 MPa plate reaction contains
• The 300 MPa stop criterion reads the plate reaction during compression, which includes global 
viscous damping: in one 7:3 bed the drag is 57.9 % of the target force (750 N, deck units).
• At fixed platen the same bed relaxes to 165 MPa; a servo branch holding the target force 
(damping 1e-5) instead compacts it further (111.05 → 105.84 µm) — model-internal until the 
open checks pass.

Next: in progress — dry mixing before pressing

12Battery Materials Lab.
 Layered-bed mixing: unresolved mixing-index contrast
• Rotating-drum DEM, cohesive soft contacts: ten runs from a layered start, eight revolutions; 
Lacey index M on 16×16×4 bins vs a random reference.
• Low NCM–NCM cohesion versus the reference setting gives an unresolved paired contrast at 
16×16×4 bins (ΔM = 0.0012, seed SE = 0.0073). Subsequent diagnostic classification; the 
original 1% overlap condition was not met.

Next: exploratory cohesion settings

13Battery Materials Lab.
 Exploratory cohesion settings produce different mixing indices
• One seed, two revolutions: large-NCM self-pair model Bond number 38.4, 384, 1152, or all 
nonzero cohesion-energy densities ×10 and ×14.42 (vs the low-cohesion comparator).
• Within each series ΔM rises with the imposed level; levels were chosen post hoc, and wall 
adhesion and start states also differ — no verdict.

Next: why SE–SE adhesion is the open term

14Battery Materials Lab.
 Surface energy and coating: SE–SE adhesion is the open term
• With equal contact areas and an assumed geometric-mean adhesion rule, ΔW = 2(√γ_A − 
√γ_S)² ≥ 0 is an adhesive-work difference per unit area; SE–SE cluster survival also depends on 
relative surface energies and contact dynamics.
• Exploratory all-pair CED scaling retains a larger SE–SE cluster fraction than the low-cohesion 
comparator; the confirmatory 18-run block remains on hold.
Mixing
This work: exploratory contact statistics (left), conditional adhesion model (right)
Left: one seed, mean over the second revolution; whiskers = dump-resolution range, not a confidence interval.
Right: γ = surface energy, W = work of adhesion; the uncoated NCM / SE surface-energy ratio is not known.
Literature: fines adhering to carriers — ordered mixing [4], interactive mixture [5]; clean-slab DFT γ: LiNiO₂ < LiCoO₂ [7]

Next: summary of findings and limitations

16Battery Materials Lab.
Summary
 Current findings and limitations
• DEM and contact networks: composition trends from one bed per composition
• DEM loading: the nominal 300 MPa plate reaction includes damping; a revised protocol is 
planned
• MPM: plastic deformation, with compaction agreement dependent on initialization and loading 
protocol
• Voxel transport: ideal-interface calculations with grid dependence and unresolved absolute 
conductivity
• Mixing: unresolved diagnostic mixing-index contrast under an unmet overlap condition; 
exploratory cohesion results without a verdict
• Final model-validation verdicts remain pending
